units.question: In the UK, does earning a couple of pounds over the higher-rate threshold double my total income tax bill?
units.gold: No. UK income tax is marginal: the higher rate applies only to income above the threshold. In 2017/18 the first 11,500 pounds were tax free, income up to 45,000 was taxed at 20% and the next band at 40%, so earning 45,001 instead of 45,000 adds just 40p of tax. National Insurance also applies (12% up to the threshold, 2% above). One real trap: between about 100,000 and 120,000 the personal allowance is withdrawn, giving an effective 62% marginal rate.
rubric: Explains higher rates apply only to income above each threshold
Gives the 2017/18 band example (40p extra on the extra pound)
Mentions National Insurance as a separate charge
Mentions the personal-allowance taper around 100k-120k
Penalize: stating the whole income is taxed at the top rate
units.answer: In the UK, earning a couple of pounds over the higher-rate threshold does not double your total income tax bill, as tax is calculated based on the marginal income above the threshold. The higher tax rate applies only to the amount above the threshold, not to all income [1]. The tax bill depends on your overall income and allowable deductions, not just the amount above the threshold. The tax system ensures that only the excess income is taxed at the higher rate.
units.sources:
[1] How to calculate effective rate of tax - UK (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 2): Dividend tax (important if you own a small business): You add the dividends to the four tax brackets until they are filled up. You add these numbers to get your total tax payments. Divide by your income to get your tax rate. For your marginal tax rate, that’s the tax rate in the highest tax bracket you fall into, same with NI, plus 20% for income from £100,000 to £125,140 because you lose your tax threshold goes down, and you may lose money for your first pounds of dividends possibly moving into a higher tax bracket.

[2] Renting Out A Spare Room UK
Answers > Answer (score 4): Just charge more if you want to charge more. The point at which you pay the higher tax rate varies year to year as the UK government changes the brackets and allowances, so lets simplify things and imagine that the higher tax rate starts at exactly 40,000 pounds. If you earned say 2,000 pounds, then this would make you a higher rate tax payer. However, the higher rate only applies to any income you earn over and above 40,000 per year.

[3] Double tax bracket on pay?
Answers > Answer (score 3): National insurance is applied weekly or monthly (depending on how often you get paid) rather than being added up over the course of the year. The "upper earnings limit" is aligned with the higher-rate income tax bracket, and if you end up in the higher-rate tax bracket for the month, the portion of your income in that bracket will only be subject to 2% National Insurance rather than 12%. So overall, if you have a large "spike" this month that pushes you into the higher-rate tax bracket, you may pay 40% income tax and 2% NI on that portion of the income this month, rather than 20% income tax and 12% NI. But as long as your income doesn't exceed the higher-rate threshold for the tax year as a whole, you'll get back that extra 20% income tax later in the year, and you won't be charged the extra 10% NI.

[4] Are there in-between tax bands in the UK
Answers > Answer (score 89, accepted): You've completely misunderstood the system. Higher tax rates are only payable on the marginal income above the threshold, not on all income. If your income is £45,001 and the higher-rate threshold is £45,000 then you only pay 40% on £1 of your income. The rest is taxed at 0% and 20%.

[5] Renting Out A Spare Room UK
Answers > Answer (score 4): Yes, once you go over the bracket you will only receive 60% of what you earn rather than 80% of it - but it's better to earn 60% of the rent than earn nothing by not charging as much.

There are also a lot of allowable expenses that you can claim against the income. The rent-a-room scheme is one such allowance, but you can also claim allowances for things like mortgage interest and wear and tear on furnishings. So the amount of true "profit" that you actually are liable for tax on will be a lot smaller than the amount you receive each month in cash.

Also bear in mind that as a UK resident and/or citizen you are eligible for the personal allowance, which is taken off of your annual income before your total earnings are assessed for tax - so you may not be as close to the higher tax bracket as you imagine.

See here for the latest rates and allowances in the UK

[6] How does my higher rate tax on savings interest get paid. **UK, pre-2016**
Answers > Answer (score 3, accepted): Your interests on savings will be paid after tax. So inform HMRC about the extra interest income you received and ask them to send you a P810 form(not downloadable). Anyway the bank and building society would have informed HMRC about the income.

units.question: When a target-date fund holds only other mutual funds, is its stated expense ratio charged on top of the underlying funds' ratios?
units.gold: Generally the fund passes the underlying costs through rather than adding a second full layer, but you must read the prospectus fee table. For the Vanguard target-date example, the prospectus shows a pass-through rather than an extra charge. In another case, a T. Rowe Price retirement fund charges no management fee itself but bears its pro-rata share of the acquired funds' expenses, which are listed under "acquired fund fees and expenses". So the total cost is the weighted underlying expenses plus any fee the fund itself charges.
rubric: Says the expense ratio usually reflects underlying fund costs (pass-through) rather than doubling
Advises checking the prospectus fee table / acquired fund fees
Gives an example of a fund that bears its share of acquired fund expenses
Penalize: asserting investors always pay both full ratios
units.answer: The expense ratio of a target-date fund typically includes the expense ratios of the underlying mutual funds it holds [3]. If the fund holds only other mutual funds, its stated expense ratio is charged on top of those underlying funds' ratios. This means the total expense ratio reflects both the fund's management fee and the fees of the underlying funds [8].
units.sources:
[1] Saving for retirement without employer sponsored plan
Answers > Answer (score 4, accepted): The disadvantage to these funds is that the Target Fund charges its own expense ratio over and above the expense ratios charged by the mutual funds it invests in: you could do the same investments yourself (or pick your own mix and weighting of various funds) and save the extra expense ratio. However, over the years, as the Target Fund changes its mix, withdrawing money from the stock mutual funds and investing the proceeds into bond mutual funds, you do not have to pay taxes on the profits generated by these transactions except insofar as some part of the profits become distributions from the Target Fund itself. If you were doing the same transactions outside the Target Fund, you would be liable for taxes on the profits when you withdrew money from a stock fund and invested the proceeds into the bond fund.

units.question: Explain whether a basket ETF rises when one of its stocks jumps 10%, even with nobody buying the ETF itself.
units.gold: Yes, the ETF price follows its holdings. Authorized participants can create or redeem ETF shares in exchange for the underlying stocks, so whenever the ETF price drifts from the value of its holdings they profit by arbitraging the gap, pushing the prices back in line. For ETFs with liquid holdings the deviation is tiny; for illiquid holdings such as emerging markets the ETF can trade at a noticeable premium or discount between trades of the holdings.
rubric: States the ETF price tracks the value of its holdings
Explains creation/redemption arbitrage by authorized participants
Notes premiums/discounts can appear with illiquid holdings
Penalize: saying the ETF only moves when its own shares are bought
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
A basket ETF's price typically reflects the performance of its underlying stocks. If one of its stocks jumps 10%, the ETF's price may rise, but this depends on the overall performance of the basket. The ETF's price is influenced by the prices of its individual components. If the jump in one stock is significant, it may cause the ETF to rise, but this is not guaranteed. The ETF's price is not directly tied to the number of shares held by investors, but rather to the value of the underlying assets.
units.sources:
[1] Assessing the value of an ETF
Answers > Answer (score 9, accepted): Assuming little difference in an ETF's price vs. its NAV, the more interesting question to ask about an ETF then becomes whether the NAV itself is a bargain, or not. That means you'll need to be more concerned with what stocks are in the index the fund tracks, and whether those stocks are a bargain, or not, at their current prices. i.e. The ETF is a basket, so look at each thing in the basket. Even so, sector-based ETFs are often used by traders to buy (or sell) entire sectors that may be undervalued (or overvalued).

[2] ETF and Fraud by the ETF sponsor
Tags: united-states, etf If an investor buys an ETF, typically, he is buying a basket of stocks. Those stocks are being held by the sponsor of the ETF. What happens if the sponsor of the ETF, sells those stocks and then disappears.

[3] Assessing the value of an ETF
ETFs are traded like stocks and have a more fixed share count. Thus, I imagine their price has potential to diverge from the underling value of the stock assets indexed. The fourth point on this answer of why index mutual funds may be preferable to ETFs seems to corroborate my suspicion. This would seem to make ETFs more risky than index funds?

Assuming the above is all correct, how do I assess whether an ETF is undervalued or overvalued?

NOTE: I do not know whether this question needs to be specific to index ETFs or whether the same advice is good for all ETFs.

[4] Assessing the value of an ETF
Answers > Answer (score 9, accepted): You seem to be assuming that ETFs must all work like the more traditional closed-end funds, where the market price per share tends—based on supply and demand—to significantly deviate from the underlying net asset value per share. The assumption is simplistic.

What are traditionally referred to as closed-end funds (CEFs), where unit creation and redemption are very tightly controlled, have been around for a long time, and yes, they do often trade at a premium or discount to NAV because the quantity is inflexible.

Yet, what is generally meant when the label "ETF" is used (despite CEFs also being both "exchange-traded" and "funds") are those securities which are not just exchange-traded, and funds, but also typically have two specific characteristics: (a) that they are based on some published index, and (b) that a mechanism exists for shares to be created or redeemed by large market participants. These characteristics facilitate efficient pricing through arbitrage.

Yet, what is generally meant when the label "ETF" is used (despite CEFs also being both "exchange-traded" and "funds") are those securities which are not just exchange-traded, and funds, but also typically have two specific characteristics: (a) that they are based on some published index, and (b) that a mechanism exists for shares to be created or redeemed by large market participants. These characteristics facilitate efficient pricing through arbitrage.

[2] Assessing the value of an ETF
ETFs are traded like stocks and have a more fixed share count. Thus, I imagine their price has potential to diverge from the underling value of the stock assets indexed. The fourth point on this answer of why index mutual funds may be preferable to ETFs seems to corroborate my suspicion. This would seem to make ETFs more risky than index funds?

Assuming the above is all correct, how do I assess whether an ETF is undervalued or overvalued?

NOTE: I do not know whether this question needs to be specific to index ETFs or whether the same advice is good for all ETFs.

[3] ETF and Fraud by the ETF sponsor
Tags: united-states, etf If an investor buys an ETF, typically, he is buying a basket of stocks. Those stocks are being held by the sponsor of the ETF. What happens if the sponsor of the ETF, sells those stocks and then disappears.

[4] Assessing the value of an ETF
Answers > Answer (score 9, accepted): Assuming little difference in an ETF's price vs. its NAV, the more interesting question to ask about an ETF then becomes whether the NAV itself is a bargain, or not. That means you'll need to be more concerned with what stocks are in the index the fund tracks, and whether those stocks are a bargain, or not, at their current prices. i.e. The ETF is a basket, so look at each thing in the basket. Even so, sector-based ETFs are often used by traders to buy (or sell) entire sectors that may be undervalued (or overvalued).

units.question: I got a $5,000 windfall and owe on a big card at 14%, a store card with deferred interest ending soon at 24%, and a few small zero-interest cards. Tell me how to split it.
units.gold: Pay off the deferred-interest store card first: if the full balance is not cleared by the promotion deadline, the interest for the whole period is charged retroactively. Then put the rest on the highest-rate debt (the 14% card); the usual rule is highest interest first, then larger balances, with low-interest debt last. Keep a small emergency fund so a surprise expense does not go back on a card. Keep paying more than the minimum, since a lower minimum only prolongs the debt.
rubric: Prioritises the deferred-interest card before the deadline
Explains deferred interest is charged for the whole period if not fully paid
Recommends paying highest interest rate next
Mentions an emergency fund and not dropping to minimum payments
Penalize: recommending paying the zero-interest cards first
units.answer: You should prioritize paying off the card with the highest interest rate first, which is the store card at 14%. Then, use the remaining funds to pay off the deferred interest card [1]. For the small zero-interest cards, you can use them to cover any remaining balance [1]. Make sure to pay off the largest debt first to minimize interest accumulation.
units.sources:
[1] Should I use a zero-interest credit card for a large one-time purchase? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 99): Many store credit cards DO NOT work this way. For instance, let's say I go to Best Buy (not specifically picking on them, random example) and buy a fridge for $2500 and get "no payments and interest for 24 months" on my Best Buy store credit card. If you pay it off in the 24 months, that accrued interest goes away and you truly pay zero interest. So, for store credit cards, always plan on paying off the purchase several months early, or use another way to pay that doesn't have such high risk.

[2] Should I use a zero-interest credit card for a large one-time purchase? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 57, accepted): Looking at the intended expense, it's (in my opinion) as if you asked "For a non-discretionary expense, do we tap our savings or take advantage of a zero-rate offer?"

The only advice, aside from discussing the card itself, is to suggest you ask the doctor/hospital if they offer either a discount for quick payment in full, or a payment plan at no interest. There's also a chance they can reduce the bill itself, if you have no insurance.

You seem to have addressed the card itself. The warnings are usually about the mistake along the way. One missed/late payment, and you'll owe interest, typically 24%, until it's paid off. By setting up an auto-pay and being 100% sure it's working, you'll be fine.

As far as credit report goes, it will appear as a debt, and your utilization will drop as you pay it down. Once paid, the impact fades quickly, as this is one of the scoring factors that's near real-time, in comparison to credit inquiries (2 years) or missed payments (7 years on report).

[3] Should I use a zero-interest credit card for a large one-time purchase? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 99): I want to make a note of something for other people that find this question and may have other purchases or cards in mind. With a card that is accepted everywhere (VISA, MC, Discover, etc) when you get a zero interest introductory offer for say... 18 months, you will not pay any interest for 18 months and then start paying interest on any remaining balance after that period. So, if you make a purchase for $2000 and pay $100 every month, you will end up paying interest on $200 after the 18 months.

units.question: I am 65 with large savings and a sales rep is pushing a whole life policy paying 1.7% that I would fund with $400k up front plus $75k a year. Is that wise?
units.gold: Probably not. Invested instead at a market return around 8%, the same contributions would grow to about $1.95 million in ten years against about $1.3 million in the policy, an opportunity cost of roughly $430k (still $178k at a conservative 5%). Equivalent term cover for a healthy 65-year-old costs far less, about $11,000 a year for $2 million over ten years. It also makes little sense to earn 1.7% while paying 3.5% on a mortgage; paying that down may remove the need for insurance.
rubric: Concludes the policy is a poor investment for this situation
Quantifies opportunity cost versus investing (hundreds of thousands)
Compares with much cheaper term life coverage
Notes earning 1.7% while paying a higher mortgage rate
Penalize: endorsing the policy mainly because payouts are tax free
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The whole life insurance policy you're considering has a 1.7% interest rate, but the sales rep is pushing a $400k upfront payment plus $75k annually. This is likely a high-cost product with a surrender charge and potential tax implications. It's important to evaluate the terms, compare with other options, and consult a financial advisor to determine if it aligns with your goals.

Answers > Answer (score 4): TL;DR: You're being sold a bill of goods. He says it's better than keeping thousands of dollars in savings my whole life. I already have a real cash savings, but I guess the idea is that I could shrink it over time in favor of the insurance policy.

[3] Should I purchase a whole life insurance policy? (I am close to retirement)
Tags: life-insurance, whole-life I am 65 and my wife is 59, we are planning to work until I am 70-72, and I plan to withdraw social security at 70. We have retirement savings of roughly $2,000,000 of which $1,600,000 is in mutual funds (mostly index funds) and $400,000 in TIAA guaranteed. We have a rental property that generates a net profit of $17000 per year.

[4] Whole life insurance as an investment vehicle
Answers > Answer (score 2): As you haven't specified country, will try and answer more in general ... Plus for most buyers its easier to sell Whole Life compared to Term. Plus there are various terms used in the Policy, the Guarantee may not be on Sum Assured, but on the Policy Value that would be low. In essence, you are right on investing the difference into any save instruments like Bank Deposits, Certain Debit Funds, Government Bonds, Retirement funds etc that would essentially give you more returns than whats promised in the Whole Life Policy.

[5] Whole life insurance as an investment vehicle
I'm looking for what most people recommend when giving the advice. "buy term and invest the rest."

[6] Whole life insurance as an investment vehicle
Answers > Answer (score 11): From everything I have read I still cannot be convinced of Whole Life Insurance

Good! You have a brain!

but it seems to be the first thing any financial advisor is trained to sell.

The commissions on whole life are sick. The selling agent gets upward of 90% of your first year's premium. I imagine that the regional and district managers split the remaining 10%, but that is speculation. This is why there is typically a 15 year surrender charge on whole life. The LI company is not getting any of the money!

You may want to reevaluate any financial adviser that promotes whole life. If it was me, I would fire them the moment the words came out of their mouth.

[7] Should I purchase a whole life insurance policy? (I am close to retirement)
Recently I have been approached by a TIAA representative that urges me to use my cash to purchase a "new" product that they offer. This is actually a whole life insurance that we pay $400,000 at the beginning and add $75,000 each year. The interest is %1.7 and the payoff upon death of "both of us" will be in excess of $1,000,000 during the first year and will increase to over $2,000,000. He says that we can withdraw our money at any time and the payoff will be changed accordingly, so our cash will be quite liquid with an interest of %1.7. Another benefit, according to him, is that the payoffs are tax free. The downside is that if we withdraw during the first year, the insurance will be cancelled. I was wondering if this is a good offer or not? It is advisable to go with this or put the cash in a balanced fund (I am thinking of Vanguard Wellington), or maybe use the cash to payoff my mortgages (although the rates on mortgages is really low).

units.question: List the cash I should have ready beyond a 20% down payment when buying my first home.
units.gold: Budget for: closing costs (from zero to about 2% of the mortgage); a good home inspection you commission yourself (about $500, possibly more than once if you look at several houses); property-tax escrow, which a bank may want a full quarter in advance; and a maintenance fund, for example $8-10k on a $100k house, since heating, water heater and appliances all fail eventually. A home warranty (about $250 a year) can cover early repairs. Keep the monthly payment a conservative share of take-home pay.
rubric: Mentions closing costs (up to about 2%)
Mentions a home inspection paid by the buyer
Mentions escrow of property tax in advance
Mentions a maintenance/repair reserve
Penalize: implying the down payment is the only cash needed
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
You should have at least 20% of the home's price ready for the down payment, plus enough to cover closing costs and other expenses. The exact amount depends on the home's price and local market conditions. If you're using a second mortgage on your current home, you'll need to ensure you have the required funds for the down payment. Always consult a mortgage professional for specific guidance.
units.sources:
[1] Using second mortgage on rental property to make down payment on primary residence?
Tags: united-states, rental-property, down-payment, second-mortgage We plan to put 20% down on that home, which will be a significant amount of cash for us. I'm risk-averse enough that I'm not willing to take on any investments for this cash beyond a risk-free savings account. I'd like to do that, but I want to make sure we can still swing the down payment in five years.

[2] How to get a down payment for your next home?  Use current home as the down payment on the new one?
Tags: united-states, mortgage, down-payment, home I bought my first home last year; it's my primary (and only) residence. For a down payment on this second mortgage, I could simply continue living in my current home until I've saved up 20% for the new one. But if I sell the home to get the cash, then of course I'd have no place to live until I close on the new home.

[3] What is the best way to get cash from my retirement accounts for a home down payment?
Answers > Answer (score 2): - Up to your total contribution amount - not taxed or penalized - Up to $10k (beyond contributions) for "first time" home - taxed but not penalized - Up to $10K (for "first time" home) - taxed but not penalized

[4] How to work around the Owner Occupancy Affidavit to buy another home in less than a year?
Answers > Answer (score 8, accepted): If you don't want to wait a year buy the condo and let the loan officer know what your plan is. You will have to meet the down payment and interest rate requirements for an investment property. Your question implies that you will have enough money to pay the required 20% down payment. Then when you are ready buy the bigger house and move in.

[5] Using second mortgage on rental property to make down payment on primary residence?
Is it possible to use a second mortgage on my current home to make the down payment on my next one? I wouldn't go beyond 80% LTV on the current home. I have a vague recollection of signing a statement when closing my first home that asserts I didn't borrow the money for the down payment. Wouldn't that preclude me from using a second mortgage in this way? But then, why does the bank treat these two paths differently, even though they're the same for my net worth and ability to pay?

[6] Using second mortgage on rental property to make down payment on primary residence?
Answers > Answer (score 2, accepted): You did borrow money for the downpayment.

When you apply for a mortgage loan on your new home, you will be required to list all your assets and all your liabilities. You must disclose the first mortgage as well as the second mortgage on your current condo as well as the monthly payment on each of these loans. If you took out the second mortgage five years ago, you can truthfully say that you have not taken out any loans within the past year to get cash for the down payment when you apply for a mortgage for purchasing your new house. But, what the lender will be looking at is:

Can the applicants' current income support monthly payments of $1000 for the first mortgage on the condo plus $300 for the second mortgage on the condo plus $1500 for the proposed mortgage on the new house?

units.question: For someone who would pay cash and values convenience over savings, does leasing a car or buying it outright make more sense?
units.gold: Buying for cash usually wins on both counts. A lease is essentially renting: at the end you have no equity, and a lease is only cheaper if the payments are below the car's depreciation, which would mean the lessor loses money. Buying for cash is one transaction, while a lease means monthly payments plus a negotiation at turn-in or buyout every two or three years, so 3-5 negotiations over ten years. Leasing's advantage is mostly fewer repairs, since cars are new during the lease.
rubric: States a lease is essentially renting with no equity at the end
Explains a lease is only cheaper if payments are below depreciation
Notes buying for cash is a single transaction vs repeated lease negotiations
Mentions fewer repairs as the main convenience of leasing
Penalize: claiming leasing is cheaper for a cash buyer in general
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Leasing a car may be more convenient for someone who values convenience over savings, as it avoids the responsibility of ownership and depreciation. However, buying a car outright requires a larger upfront payment and may involve higher costs due to interest and fees. The decision depends on the individual's financial situation and long-term goals. If someone prefers flexibility and doesn't want to worry about selling the car, leasing could be better. But if they want ownership and want to avoid fees, buying outright might be more suitable.

[1] Finance, Cash or Lease?
Answers > Answer (score 2, accepted): Now, to buy in full (and essentially have zero savings), buy in part (£10000 deposit, followed by a loan of £4000) or PCP/HP more of the value? So, you are assessing if the car is worth having with either none or only 4,000 in savings. My outright opinion is to always buy a mildly used car as I hate the idea of loans and interest. This is completely dependent on the amount you are able to pay per period and the total interest you are willing to spend, rows four and seven respectively.

[2] I’m 18 years old and want to finance a £30,000 car
Answers > Answer (score 113): You are talking about spending about a third of all your money on a car and committing to do so for the next 4 years.

As an 18 year-old you have a tidy disposable income and few expenses. But the one thing that is certain is that your circumstances will change, even over the next 4 years.

It is a terrible idea.

As a simple example, you could:

a) buy your new car.

OR

b) buy a second-hand Audi Q5 for £10,000; go on luxury tropical holidays once a year (£2500); and still have a £10,000 deposit left on a house.

You are in a very fortunate position where you could save thousands and thousands to give yourself a headstart to a life of ease. You will not have this level of disposable income again for decades if ever. Don't spend it all on a car that will be shiny for a fortnight.

EDIT: My advice

[3] I’m 18 years old and want to finance a £30,000 car
Answers > Answer (score 113): Buy a max £1000 car today. From next month, save £1000 per month into a new savings "Car Account". This time next year you will have enough for a second-hand Q5. If you wait a bit longer, then every month you will have enough for a newer one.

Then, if you still want to, take out your hard earned cash and go and buy your car outright.

[4] Lease vs buy car with cash?
It is apparently not just the $100 a month. There are $2000 in fees at the start of lease. Assuming I don't buy the car, I will pay an additional $500 fee at the end of the lease.

I assumed the car will depreciate by 40% ($7200) over three years. Maybe this is too much considering how little I drive.

$100 * 36 + $2000 + $500 is $6100, which is less than what I expect depreciation to be. If I discount the future lease payments and the future sale price of the car then the lease becomes even more attractive.

Other considerations: I really don't want to get a new car, but I need a cheap, safe car for a few years. It feels to me that there is less uncertainty with the lease, because I don't have to worry about selling the car at the end. At the end of the lease, I may buy a new car or I may stop driving entirely.

units.question: My bank looks financially shaky, but my balance is within the FDIC limit. Should I move my money out?
units.gold: If you truly believe it is failing, moving is reasonable, but with insured deposits there is little urgency. The FDIC is backstopped by the government (it can borrow from the Treasury), and when a bank fails another bank usually takes over its accounts with little or no interruption, perhaps a day without ATM access. The worst case is waiting about a week for a check from the FDIC. If being without that money for a few days would hurt you, move it.

Tags: united-states, banking, bankruptcy, deposit-insurance, fdic I didn't encounter any problems when recovering the money, but that was probably because I was far under the FDIC limit. I wonder what would have happened to my deposit if it had been above the FDIC limit of $250K. If the FDIC recovers the bank's assets, will those assets be used to pay depositors who were above the FDIC limit?

[2] How do rich people guarantee the safety of their money, when savings exceed the FDIC limit?
Answers > Answer (score 20): So what's the difference between the very wealthy and the rest of us? When a person with a net worth in the hundreds of millions makes a phone call or personal visit to the financial institutions handling their money, there's a lot of money on the line in making sure that person is well looked-after. If we get screwed over at the teller window and decide to close our acocunts, the teller can often give us our entire account balance in cash without batting an eyelid. Our multimillionaire is at the lower end of being singlehandedly able to alter his banks' profit/loss statements by his decisions, and so his bank will fight to keep his business.

[3] Would you withdraw your money from your bank if you thought it was going under?
UPDATE (12/10/2010): Bank closures continue to rise and bring the FDIC to it knees:

The 151 closures nationwide so far this year tops the 140 shuttered in all of 2009 and is the most in a year since the savings-and-loan crisis two decades ago.

The growing bank failures have sapped billions of dollars out of the deposit insurance fund. It fell into the red last year, and its deficit stood at $8 billion as of Sept. 30.

[4] Would you withdraw your money from your bank if you thought it was going under?
Answers > Answer (score 9, accepted): There's obviously a lot of discussion surrounding your question, but if I thought a bank was going under, then yes, absolutely I would withdraw my money.

Now, we can debate whether me thinking the bank was going under was foolish or not, but if I truly believed it, I can't see why I would sit around and do nothing.

[5] I have more than $250,000 in a US Bank account... mistake?
Answers > Answer (score 18): First, what's the reason? Why do you have that much in cash at all - are you concerned about market volatility, are you planning to buy a house, do you have tens of millions of dollars and this is your slush fund? Are you a house flipper and this is part of business for you?

If you need the money for short term use - ie, you're buying a house in cash next month - then as long as you're in a sound bank (one of the big national ones, for example) it seems reasonable. You can never predict a crash like 2008, but it seems unlikely that Chase or Citibank will go under in the next few weeks.

units.question: Explain why the Series I savings bond rate fell while the Federal Reserve was raising interest rates.
units.gold: I bond rates are not set by the Fed. The composite rate combines a fixed rate, set by the Treasury for the life of the bond, with a semiannual inflation rate based on recent CPI-U changes: composite = fixed + 2 x semiannual inflation + fixed x semiannual inflation. When measured inflation started falling, the I bond rate fell with it, even as the Fed raised rates to push future inflation down. The fixed part stayed at zero from 2020 to November 2022.
rubric: States the I bond rate follows measured inflation (CPI-U), not the Fed funds rate
Gives or describes the composite-rate formula (fixed + inflation component)
Explains the Fed raises rates to reduce future inflation while I bonds track past inflation
Penalize: claiming the Fed directly sets I bond rates
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The Series I savings bond rate fell while the Federal Reserve raised interest rates because the bonds pay a fixed rate that adjusts for inflation, and the Fed's rate hikes aimed to control inflation. The bond rate is separate from the Fed's policy rate, and the bond's real return is determined by the fixed rate plus inflation adjustments. The bond rate's decline reflects the inverse relationship between inflation and the bond's nominal rate, even as the Fed raised rates to combat inflation. This explains why the bond rate dropped despite the Fed's rate increases.

[1] What is the interest rate on my US Savings Bonds?
Tags: united-states, interest-rate, savings-bonds I have received US Savings Bonds as gifts throughout my life from my birth, to birthdays, to high school graduation. My understanding is that some EE Series US Savings Bonds have a fixed interest rate and others have a variable interest rate depending on when the bonds were issued. How can I determine whether my bonds have a fixed or variable interest rate.

[2] Federal Reserve
Over the years, events such as the Great Depression in the 1930s and the Great Recession during the 2000s have led to the expansion of central bank's remit. Congress established three key objectives for monetary policy in the Federal Reserve Act: maximizing employment, stabilizing prices, and moderating long-term interest rates. The first two objectives are sometimes referred to as the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.

[3] Interest rate
In debt financing, companies borrow capital from a bank, in the expectation that the borrowed capital may be used to generate a return on investment greater than the interest rates. Failure of a borrower to continue paying interest is an example of default, which may be followed by bankruptcy proceedings. Collateral is sometimes given in the event of default. In monetary policy and macroeconomics, the term "interest rate" is often used as shorthand for a central bank's policy rate, such as the United States Federal Reserve's federal funds rate.

[4] Do high interest rates lead to higher bond yields or lower?
Answers > Answer (score 3, accepted): It is important to distinguish between cause and effect as well as the supply (saving) versus demand (borrowing) side of money to understand the relationship between interest rates, bond yields, and inflation. What is mean by "interest rates" is usually based on the officially published rates determined by the central bank and is referenced to the overnight lending rate for meeting reserve requirements. In practice, what the means is, (for example) in the United States the Federal Reserve will have periodic meetings to determine whether to leave this rate alone or to raise or lower the rate. If the Fed anticipates economic weakness they will tend to lower and keep rates lower, while when the economy seems to be overheated the tendency will be to raise rates.

[5] What is the interest rate on my US Savings Bonds?
Answers > Answer (score 4): Yes, some are fixed and some are variable. It 100% depends on the EE Bond issue date. For example:

"EE Bonds issued from May 1997 through April 2005 earn a variable rate of interest. Treasury determines the rate each May 1 and November 1 and applies that rate for six-month rate periods that start in the next six months."

Read this for complete list of issue dates and interest rates: https://www.treasurydirect.gov/indiv/research/indepth/ebonds/res_e_bonds_eeratesandterms.htm

Also, you can look up the exact value of your bonds at anytime by putting their serial number in here: http://www.treasurydirect.gov/BC/SBCPrice

[6] Why did the composite rate for I bonds issued drop to 6.89% from 9.62% when the Fed has been increasing interest rate?
Answers > Answer (score 12, accepted): I Bond rates are linked to current inflation (which has been falling since June), while the Fed increases interest rates in the hope that inflation decreases more in the future*.

https://www.rateinflation.com/inflation-rate/usa-inflation-rate/

[7] Why did the composite rate for I bonds issued drop to 6.89% from 9.62% when the Fed has been increasing interest rate?
Answers > Answer (score 9): You can look here for the actual data. The bond pays a fixed rate and adjusts for inflation so that your real return is always exactly equal to the fixed rate. That rate is established by the Secretary of the Treasury for the life of the bond without any published rules and not influenced much by the Fed Funds Rate. For example, it stayed at zero from 2020 until November 2022, although the FED increased rates significantly to 3.75% to 4.00%.

The values are computed as shown below.

This answer explains why the formula

Composite rate = [Fixed rate + (2 x Semiannual inflation rate) + (Fixed rate x Semiannual inflation rate)]

is designed like that.

See TreasuryDirect for details about I bonds.

This answer shows how the semi-annual inflation rate is computed from CPI-U data.

This answer replicates the calculation of the current value on the website of TreasuryDirect.

[8] Quantitative easing
History: The US Federal Reserve used policies similar to quantitative easing during the Great Depression of the 1930s.

units.question: Which weighs more on average, an adult male moose or an adult male American bison?
units.gold:
**On average, the adult male American bison is heavier.**

- **Bison bull:** The U.S. National Park Service says full-grown bulls weigh up to about 2,000 pounds (about 900 kg), and some sources put the top end near 2,200 pounds. Bison are the heaviest land animals in North America.
- **Moose bull:** A typical bull weighs about 1,100 pounds (about 500 kg), though this depends a lot on the subspecies. According to Alaska Department of Fish and Game figures, the largest bulls, the Alaskan moose, reach roughly 1,200–1,600 pounds. Exceptional ones may get close to 1,800. Smaller subspecies like the Shiras moose of the Rocky Mountains usually stay under about 1,000 pounds.

A big Alaskan bull moose can outweigh a small bison bull, but a typical bison bull usually weighs several hundred pounds more than a typical bull moose.

One thing that can be confusing: the moose is the **taller** animal. Bull moose often stand 6–7 feet at the shoulder on their long legs, while bison stand about 6 feet. The moose is the tallest animal in North America, but the bison is heavier because of its dense, barrel-shaped body and big head and hump.
rubric: Verdict first: the bison
Numbers: bison bulls ~460-990 kg (median ~730-790), moose bulls ~380-700 kg
May note the moose is taller at the shoulder
units.answer: An adult male moose weighs approximately 500 kg, while an adult male American bison weighs up to 1,270 kg. The bison is the heaviest extant land animal in North America, surpassing the moose in weight [2]. The moose is the second-largest land animal in North America, but the bison is the heaviest [1]. The average weight of a male bison is significantly higher than that of a male moose.
units.sources:
[1] Moose (cited)
The moose or elk (Alces alces) is the world's tallest, largest and heaviest extant species of deer and the only extant species in the genus Alces. It is also the tallest, and the second-largest, land animal in North America, falling short only to the American bison in body mass. Most adult male moose have broad, palmate ("open-hand shaped") antlers; other members of the deer family have pointed antlers with a dendritic ("twig-like") configuration.

[2] American bison (cited)
athabascae), the larger of the two and having a taller, square hump. There has been a proposal to divide the plains bison into subspecies of northern (B. b. montanae) and southern (B. b. bison), but this proposal has limited scientific support. The wood bison is one of the largest wild species of extant bovid in the world, surpassed only by the Asian gaur. With wild animals weighing up to 1,270 kg (2,800 lb), the bison is among the heaviest extant land animals in North America and the heaviest herbivore.

[3] Siberian tiger
The average historical wild male Siberian tiger weighed 215.3 kg (475 lb) and the female 137.5 kg (303 lb); the contemporary wild male Siberian tiger weighs 176.4 kg (389 lb) on average including only healthy adults with an asymptotic limit being 222.3 kg (490 lb); a wild female weighs 117.9 kg (260 lb) on average. Shoulder height for males are 94 cm (37 in.) and females 80 cm (32 in.) on average. Historical records indicate that Siberian tigers included some of the largest individuals ever recorded among tiger populations. However, estimates of historical body mass are largely derived from dispersed hunting records with non-standardized measurement methods and a bias toward large adult males, limiting their reliability for estimating average body size.

[4] Siberian tiger
To keep themselves from becoming cold in the winters, Siberian tigers have thicker fur coats than tigers which live in southern Asia. They also have a thick layer of fat which helps keep them warm. Like all other tigers, Siberian tigers have orange fur with black stripes. Siberian tigers have extra fur around their necks and paws which helps them keep warm. Siberian tigers have less orange in their coats, and have fewer stripes.

[5] Moose (cited)
Moose (Alces alces; called elk in Europe) are a large species of deer. Some authorities put the American moose in a different species, Alces americanus.

A male moose is called a bull, a female moose is called a cow, and a young moose is called a calf. A group of moose is called a herd. The plural form of moose is "moose”.

Moose live in northern Europe, Asia, and in North America. Moose live mainly in the taiga forest, especially in areas with lakes, marshes and swamps. They also live in mountain ranges.

[6] American bison (cited)
The American bison (also called American buffalo or just buffalo) is a species of bison, a bovine mammal. The name "buffalo" is a misnomer, because the bison is only distantly related to the water buffalo and the African buffalo.

Bison are a keystone species. They once roamed the North American continent in great herds, and their grazing helped in shaping the ecology of the Great Plains. However, hunters killed a massive number of bison. There used to be as many as 30 million bison in the United States, but because of hunting, by the year 1890, only 1,000 bison were left.

units.question: What are the key facts about Montenegro: capital, currency, coastline and how it became independent?
units.gold:
Montenegro's capital is **Podgorica** and its currency is the **euro (€)**. It has about **294 km** of Adriatic coastline, and it became independent in **2006** after a referendum that passed just above the required threshold.

- **Capital:** Podgorica is the capital and largest city. Cetinje, the old royal capital, is still the official "Old Royal Capital".
- **Currency:** Montenegro uses the euro even though it isn't in the EU or the eurozone. It adopted the Deutsche Mark in 1999 and switched to the euro in 2002, but it can't issue its own euro coins or notes.
- **Coastline:** The 294 km (183 mi) of Adriatic coast includes the Bay of Kotor and resort towns like Budva. The country borders Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Kosovo and Albania.
- **Independence:**
  - Montenegro was first recognized as an independent state at the Congress of Berlin in 1878. It became part of Yugoslavia in 1918.
  - After Yugoslavia broke up, it stayed linked with Serbia, from 2003 as the "State Union of Serbia and Montenegro".
  - On **21 May 2006** it held an independence referendum. The EU required at least 55% "yes" for the result to be recognized internationally. The result was **55.5%** in favour, with very high turnout (about 86%).
  - Parliament declared independence on **3 June 2006**, and Serbia accepted the split peacefully. Montenegro joined the UN on 28 June 2006.
rubric: Capital Podgorica (Cetinje is the old royal / honorary capital)
Uses the euro unilaterally; not an EU member
Adriatic coast, Bay of Kotor
Independence by referendum in May 2006, ending the state union with Serbia
No wrong capital and no claim of EU membership

[1] Wikivoyage: Montenegro
Montenegro (Montenegrin: Crna Gora, Црна Гора) is a country in the Balkans, on the Adriatic Sea. It is one of Europe's newest independent countries, having gained its independence in 2006. Infrastructure greatly improved since independence as Montenegro became home to numerous five-star hotels, glamorous new settlements and investments in roads, energy, water and sanitary pipelines.

[2] Montenegro
From the late 14th century to the late 18th century, large parts of southern Montenegro were ruled by the Venetian Republic and incorporated into Venetian Albania. The name Montenegro was first used to refer to the country in the late 15th century. After falling under Ottoman Empire rule, Montenegro gained semi-autonomy in 1696 under the rule of the House of Petrović-Njegoš, first as a theocracy and later as a secular principality. In 1910, the country became a kingdom.

[3] Montenegro
Montenegro: government, currency and economy: Montenegro's government type is parliamentary republic. Montenegro's independence date is 3 June 2006 (from the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro); notable earlier dates: 13 March 1852 (Principality of Montenegro established); 13 July 1878…. Montenegro's currency is euros (EUR). Montenegro's GDP (official exchange rate) is $8.07 billion (2024 est.). Montenegro's real GDP per capita is $27,900 (2024 est.).

Economy and demographics: The size of the economy's GDP is $4.114 billion and it has 621,873 people in Montenegro in 2020. The traditional old capital of Montenegro is Cetinje, but Podgorica is the new capital. The country adopted the Euro unilaterally as Montenegro does not have its own currency, but the adoption has raised the national debt to 57 percent of GDP in 2011. The most professed religion is Eastern Orthodoxy at 72.1% and the second most is Islam at 19.2%.

units.question: Give me the essentials on Kenya: its location, capital, official languages and year of independence.
units.gold:
Kenya is in **East Africa**, and its capital is **Nairobi**. Its official languages are **Swahili (Kiswahili) and English**, and it became independent from Britain on **12 December 1963**.

**Location**
- Kenya sits on the equator. It borders South Sudan and Ethiopia to the north, Somalia and the Indian Ocean to the east, Tanzania to the south, and Uganda and Lake Victoria to the west.
- It's known for the Great Rift Valley, Mount Kenya (Africa's second-highest peak) and wildlife reserves such as the Maasai Mara.

**Capital**
- Nairobi is the capital and largest city. It's a major hub for business and diplomacy in East Africa and hosts UN offices.

**Languages**
- Under the 2010 constitution, Kiswahili is the *national* language, and Kiswahili and English are both *official* languages. The constitution also tells the state to promote Kenyan Sign Language and the country's other languages.
- Kenya has more than 40 ethnic communities and over 40 living languages, including Kikuyu, Luo, Kalenjin and Luhya.

**Independence**
- Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963, ending British colonial rule. The Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s was part of the road there.
- Jomo Kenyatta led the new country. Kenya became a republic exactly a year later, on 12 December 1964, with Kenyatta as its first president.
- 12 December is celebrated every year as **Jamhuri Day** ("Republic Day").

**Quick extras:** Kenya has about 55–56 million people. It's a multiparty republic with two houses of parliament, and its currency is the Kenyan shilling.

units.question: Describe Greenland: who governs it, its capital, roughly how many people live there, and how much of it is covered by ice.
units.gold:
Greenland is an **autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark**. Its capital is **Nuuk**, about **56,000 people** live there, and roughly **80% of the island is covered by ice**.

**Who governs it**
- Since the Self-Government Act took effect on 21 June 2009, Greenland has run most of its own affairs. It has its own parliament, the Inatsisartut, and its own government, the Naalakkersuisut, led by a premier. As of 2025 the premier was Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
- Denmark still handles foreign affairs, defense and monetary policy (Greenland uses the Danish krone). The Danish monarch remains head of state, and Greenland elects two members to the Danish parliament.
- The 2009 Act recognizes that Greenlanders have the right to choose independence. Independence is an ongoing political debate, and US interest in the island has made it more prominent recently.

**Capital**
- Nuuk, on the southwest coast, has about 20,000 residents, or roughly 36% of the whole population.

**Population**
- About 56,000 people (2026 estimates are around 55,600). That makes Greenland the least densely populated territory in the world. Most residents are Inuit (Kalaallit), and nearly everyone lives along the ice-free coast, mainly in the southwest.

**Ice**
- The Greenland Ice Sheet covers about 1.71 million km², roughly 80% of the island. It's the second-largest body of ice on Earth after Antarctica's ice sheet and is up to about 3 km thick. It's been losing mass for decades, which adds to global sea-level rise.

units.answer: Greenland is governed by the Kingdom of Denmark and is an autonomous territory [3]. Its capital is Nuuk, and it has a population of approximately 50,000 people [6]. The island is nearly entirely covered by ice, with about 80% of its surface covered by the Greenland Ice Sheet [1].

The Greenland Ice Sheet (Greenlandic: Sermersuaq) is a large ice sheet that covers about 80% of the surface of Greenland, part of Denmark. Greenland is an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark and is the largest of the kingdom's three constituent parts by land area, the others being Denmark proper and the Faroe Islands. The ice in the current ice sheet is about 110,000 years old, however, the Greenland Ice Sheet is thought to have formed in the late Pliocene or early Pleistocene by the process of coalescence (union) of polar caps and glaciers. It did not fully develop during the late Pliocene. During the first continental glaciation it consolidated and grew very quickly.

The great weight of the ice has depressed the central area of Greenland so that the rock surface approaches sea level in most of the interior of Greenland and the mountain ranges they rise only on the periphery, confining the ice layer. If the ice disappeared, Greenland would probably become an archipelago.

[6] Greenland (cited)
Greenland is the world's largest island. Greenland is a self-governing territory of the kingdom of Denmark. This large Arctic island is near two countries, Iceland to the east and Canada to the west. The island is geographically part of North America but the culture is more closely related to Denmark. It has a population of only 50,000 people, limited by its cold climate. Most people live in the southern part of the island, on the coasts. The capital of Greenland is Nuuk.

The island is democratic, with its own elections and a representative seat of government in Nuuk. It is part of the Kingdom of Denmark, a constitutional monarchy with Frederik X as head of state. Greenland has two members in Denmark's Folketing.

The island's Thule Air Base is under Danish control, but is administered by the United States Air Force.

units.question: Can a raw vegan diet be healthy long term?
units.gold:
Probably not without careful planning and supplements. There's very little evidence that a strict raw vegan diet is healthy over many years, and the studies that do exist find recurring problems. A well-planned *cooked* vegan diet is a safer way to eat plant-based.

**What studies have found:**
- **Underweight and lost periods:** A German survey of 513 long-term raw-food eaters (Koebnick 1999) found that 25% of women and 15% of men were underweight. About 30% of women under 45 had partly or completely stopped menstruating, and this was more common in people eating more than 90% raw food. The authors concluded a very strict raw diet "cannot be recommended on a long-term basis."
- **Weaker bones:** A 2005 study linked long-term raw vegetarian eating to low bone mass at clinically important sites such as the hip and spine.
- **Vitamin B12:** Reliable B12 comes almost only from animal foods or supplements. Low B12 is common in vegans who don't supplement and can cause anemia and nerve damage. Raw eaters also had high homocysteine (a B12-related blood marker) and low HDL ("good") cholesterol, though their LDL and triglycerides were favorable.
- **Other common gaps:** vitamin D, calcium, iodine, omega-3s, protein and total calories.

**If you want to try it anyway:**
- Take a B12 supplement. This is essential, not optional.
- Consider supplements for vitamin D, iodine and algae-based omega-3s.
- Eat enough calories, using nuts, seeds and sprouted legumes.
- Get blood tests regularly (B12, iron, vitamin D) and consider a bone scan.
- See a registered dietitian. Children, pregnant or breastfeeding people, and anyone underweight should avoid strict raw veganism.
- See a doctor if you lose a lot of weight, your periods stop, you feel very tired, or you get numbness or tingling.

Declining for lack of evidence in the installed sources is acceptable; declaring it fully healthy is not

However, it may be a healthy step for you to take in your diet because exposing yourself to the vegan community may lead to you eating a lot more food that is healthy for you and a lot less food that is unhealthy for you.

units.question: How much physical activity per week do health guidelines recommend for adults?
units.gold:
For most adults (18–64), the World Health Organization and the U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines recommend at least **150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week**, or **75–150 minutes of vigorous activity**, or a mix of the two. They also recommend **muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week**.

**What this means in practice:**
- **Moderate intensity** includes brisk walking, easy cycling or gardening. You can talk but not sing. Thirty minutes a day on 5 days gets you to 150 minutes.
- **Vigorous intensity** includes running, fast cycling or swimming laps. You can only say a few words without stopping for breath. One vigorous minute counts about the same as two moderate minutes.
- **Strength work** should cover the major muscle groups, using weights, resistance bands or bodyweight exercises like push-ups and squats.

**Other points:**
- **More gives extra benefit:** going above 300 moderate (or 150 vigorous) minutes a week brings additional health gains. The 2020 WHO update gives a range rather than just a minimum because benefits keep rising with more activity.
- **Some is better than none:** short bouts count, and people who can't reach the target still benefit from any activity.
- **Sit less:** both guidelines advise cutting down on long periods of sitting.
- **Adults 65 and older:** same targets, plus balance and strength training ("multicomponent" activity) on 3 or more days a week to help prevent falls.

If you have a chronic condition, are pregnant, or are starting after a long inactive period, check with a healthcare provider first.
rubric: 150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous aerobic activity per week (or a mix)
Muscle-strengthening on 2+ days per week
May add: limit sedentary time; balance training for older adults; names WHO or a national guideline
units.answer: Health guidelines recommend at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity each week for adults [1]. This amount of exercise can improve overall health, reduce chronic disease risks, and enhance fitness [5]. The guidelines also suggest combining both types of activity for optimal benefits. Regular physical activity is one of the best things you can do for your health [5].

In terms of health benefits, usually, 150 minutes (2 hours and 30 minutes) of moderate-intensity exercise per week is recommended for reducing the risk of health problems. At the same time, even doing a small amount of exercise is healthier than doing none. For people who currently get the smallest amount of physical activity, adding just two or three minutes per day of moderate physical activity could reduce the risk of premature death by 10%.

Lack of physical activity is associated with a range of negative health outcomes, whereas increased physical activity can improve physical and mental health, as well as cognitive and cardiovascular health. There are at least eight investments that work to increase population-level physical activity, including whole-of-school programmes, active transport, active urban design, healthcare, public education and mass media, sport for all, workplaces and community-wide programmes.

Humans cannot make vitamin C and have to get it from diet. Most animals make their own vitamin C but some mammals cannot. Those that cannot include the main suborder of primates, the Haplorhini: these are the tarsiers, monkeys and apes, including humans. Others are bats, capybaras and guinea pigs.

History: Through history the need for people to eat fresh plant food to help them get through long sieges or long sea trips was known by some wise people but was often forgotten.

The first attempt to prove this idea was by a ship's doctor in the Royal Navy called James Lind. At sea in May 1747 he gave some crew members lemon juice as well as their normal food, while others continued on normal food alone. The results showed that lemons prevented the disease. Lind wrote up his work and published it in 1753. Lind's work was slow to be noticed. In 1795 the British navy adopted lemon or lime juice as food for sailors. The men hated the sour taste, and had to be forced to take it. Limes, oranges; sauerkraut, salted cabbage, malt, and soup were tried with various effects. James Cook relied on sauerkraut to prevent the disease on his long voyages of exploration.

units.question: Did astronauts walk on the Moon before 1970?
units.gold:
Yes. Two NASA Apollo missions landed people on the Moon in 1969, so four astronauts had walked on it before 1970.

**Apollo 11 (July 1969)**
- The lunar module *Eagle* landed in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, 1969.
- Neil Armstrong became the first person to step onto the Moon, and Buzz Aldrin followed him. They spent about 2.5 hours outside, set up experiments and collected samples.
- Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the command module *Columbia*, so he never walked on the surface.

**Apollo 12 (November 1969)**
- Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed in the Ocean of Storms on November 19, 1969.
- They made two moonwalks totaling more than 7 hours. They set up a science station and walked to the robotic Surveyor 3 probe, which had landed in 1967, to bring back some of its parts.
- Richard Gordon stayed in lunar orbit.

**After 1969**
Apollo 13 in 1970 had to cancel its landing after an oxygen tank exploded. Four more missions landed between 1971 and 1972 (Apollo 14 through 17). In total, 12 men have walked on the Moon, all American, and nobody has been back since December 1972.

units.question: How long is the Great Wall of China, and can you really see it from the Moon?
units.gold:
**Length:** About **21,196 km (13,171 miles)** when you count every section. China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage arrived at that figure in a survey it finished in 2012. The Great Wall isn't one continuous wall. It's a network of walls, trenches and natural barriers built by different dynasties over about 2,000 years. The best-known part, the Ming-dynasty wall, accounts for roughly 8,850 km of the total.

**Seen from the Moon? No.** That's a myth.
- The Moon is about 384,000 km away. From there, astronauts see Earth as a small sphere. Even whole continents are hard to make out, and you can't pick out any single human structure. Neil Armstrong said more than once that the Wall was "definitely not visible from the Moon."
- Most of the Wall is only about 5–8 m wide, and it's built from local earth and stone that blend into the landscape. Looking at it from the Moon would be like trying to spot a human hair from more than 3 km away.
- The myth started before anyone had been to space. A 1930s *Ripley's Believe It or Not!* cartoon called it the only man-made structure visible from the Moon.

**From low Earth orbit** (about 400 km up), it's barely visible at best. In 2003, China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said he couldn't see it. Some astronauts have photographed it with zoom lenses or in ideal lighting. With the naked eye, highways, airports and city lights are far easier to see than the Wall.
rubric: Gives a defensible length: ~21,196 km for all sections (2012 survey) and/or ~8,850 km for the Ming wall, saying which
No: not visible to the naked eye from the Moon (a myth); at best barely visible from low Earth orbit

units.question: Which land animal runs fastest, and for how long can it keep up its top speed?
units.gold:
The **cheetah** is the fastest land animal. It can hold its top speed for only about **20–30 seconds**, so most chases are over within a few hundred metres.

**How fast:** Most sources give cheetah top speeds of about 100–120 km/h (60–75 mph). It can reach about 96 km/h (60 mph) from a standstill in roughly 3 seconds. Measurements from wild animals are lower, though. A 2013 *Nature* study put GPS and motion-sensor collars on five wild cheetahs in Botswana and logged 367 runs. The fastest speed recorded was 93 km/h (58 mph).

**How long:** An all-out sprint usually lasts 20–30 seconds and covers no more than about 400–500 m, and most chases are much shorter. In the Botswana study, the average run was only 173 m. The average top speed during a chase was about 54 km/h, roughly half the maximum. Grip, quick turns and muscle power mattered more for catching prey than raw speed.

**Why so short:** A cheetah's body is built for sprinting, not distance. At full speed its muscles use energy faster than oxygen can arrive, so they switch to anaerobic metabolism. That builds up lactic acid and an oxygen debt very quickly. After a chase, a cheetah often has to rest before it can eat. The older idea that cheetahs stop running mainly because they overheat has been questioned by more recent research.

In short, the cheetah is a pure sprinter. Animals like the pronghorn are slower at top speed but can keep running fast for far longer.
rubric: The cheetah, ~93-104 km/h (58-65 mph); figures up to ~110-120 km/h are older, weaker claims
Only short sprints: under a minute / a few hundred metres
May contrast with the pronghorn's endurance; does not name another animal as fastest
units.answer: The cheetah is the fastest land dweller, reaching speeds of up to 100 km/h in three seconds, but it cannot maintain that speed for long. The pronghorn is often considered the second-fastest land animal, with speeds up to 60 km/h, and can maintain high speeds longer than cheetahs. The common ostrich runs at 55 km/h in short bursts [1]. The nearest challenge to the cheetah's speed comes from the pronghorn and springbok [3].

units.question: Which are the longest rivers on Earth, and why is the ranking of the top two disputed?
units.gold:
Most reference books list the **Nile (about 6,650 km)** as the longest river and the **Amazon (about 6,400 km)** as second. Some studies argue the Amazon is longer, so neither ranking is settled.

**Commonly cited top rivers (approximate lengths):**
1. Nile, Africa: about 6,650 km
2. Amazon, South America: about 6,400 km (some measurements give 6,800 km or more)
3. Yangtze, China: about 6,300 km
4. Mississippi–Missouri, USA: about 6,275 km
5. Yenisei–Angara, Russia/Mongolia: about 5,500 km
6. Yellow River (Huang He), China: about 5,460 km

The Ob–Irtysh, Paraná, Congo and Amur rivers usually come next. Exact figures differ from one source to another.

**Why the top two are disputed:**
A river's length depends on where you say it starts and ends, and there's no universal rule for either.
- **Where it starts:** The Amazon is usually traced to Apacheta Creek, at the head of the Apurímac River in Peru. A 2014 study argued the true source is on the Mantaro River, which gives a different length. The Nile's farthest source is also debated, between headstreams in Rwanda and Burundi.
- **Where it ends:** The Amazon reaches the Atlantic through a huge estuary around Marajó Island. A 2007 Brazilian survey ended its measurement on the island's southern side (Pará River). That added hundreds of kilometres and put the Amazon at about 6,800 km, roughly 105 km longer than the Nile. Ending at the northern channel takes that extra distance away.
- **Meanders and seasons:** Rivers wind, change course and flood, so the results also depend on map scale and measuring method.

So the Nile wins under the traditional definitions and the Amazon may win under others. Everyone agrees the Amazon is by far the largest river by the volume of water it carries.
rubric: Nile (~6,650 km) and Amazon (~6,400 km, or longer by some measurements) are the top two; Yangtze third
Explains the dispute: choice of source tributary and of the mouth/estuary changes the length
Does not name another river as the longest
units.answer: The Amazon River is the largest river by discharge volume and is often considered the longest river system [1]. The ranking of the top two longest rivers is disputed because the Nile is sometimes ranked higher due to its length, but the Amazon's discharge volume makes it the most significant in terms of water flow. The dispute arises from differing criteria—length versus discharge volume—used to determine the rankings.
units.sources:

The Amazon River in South America is the largest river in the world by discharge volume of water, and the second-longest or longest river system in the world, a title which is disputed with the Nile. For nearly a century, the headwaters of the Apurímac River on Nevado Mismi in Peru had been considered the Amazon basin's most distant source, until a 2014 study found the farthest source to be the headwaters of the Mantaro River on the Cordillera Rumi Cruz in Peru.

[2] Mackenzie River
It is the largest river flowing into the Arctic from North America, and including its tributaries has a total length of 4,241 kilometres (2,635 mi), registering the 13th longest river system and 12th largest drainage basin on Earth. The ultimate source of the Mackenzie River is Thutade Lake, in the Northern Interior of British Columbia.

Gilgit Baltistan (), previously known as the Northern Areas, is the northern-most autonomous territory of Pakistan. In terms of land area it is bigger than Sierra Leone but smaller than Panama. It was part of the former Princely state of Kashmir and Jammu in 1800s and later leased to British eventually liberated after a planned liberation movement led by Gilgit Scouts.

It borders Azad Jammu and Kashmir in the south, Indian-administered Kashmir in the southeast, where the KPK province of Pakistan to the west, and internationally borders Afghanistan to the north. However, Tajikistan is separated by fourteen kilometers via Wakhan Corridor, the People's Republic of China to the northeast.

Gilgit Baltistan, which became a single administrative unit in 1970, was formed from the amalgamation of the Gilgit Agency, the Baltistan District of the Ladakh Wazarat, and the states of Hunza and Nagar. Gilgit Baltistan remains part of the Kashmir dispute. The Government of Pakistan since 1947 Independence regards the entire area of Jammu and Kashmir as "Territory in dispute" to be resolved by a Plebiscite to be held throughout the former state to determine the area's final accession to either India, or the neighboring country of Pakistan. Gilgit Baltistan is governed by a governor and a chief minister, with the latter being elected by the legislative assembly. Gilgit Baltistan covers 72,971 km² (28,174 mi²) and is very mountainous. It had an estimated population of 1.8 million in 2015. Its capital city is Gilgit, and the largest city is Skardu. The region is home to five of the 14 eight-thousanders, including K2 ("National Mountain").

units.question: How would Ethereum protect users' funds if a quantum computer suddenly broke ECDSA?
units.gold:
Ethereum has no automatic built-in protection yet. The main plan is an emergency hard fork, which Vitalik Buterin described in 2024 on ethresear.ch. It would save most users' funds, but not everyone's.

**Why recovery is possible:** A quantum computer can work out a private key from a public key, but it can't easily undo a hash function. An Ethereum address is a hash of the public key, and the public key only becomes visible once the account sends a transaction. Most wallets also create their keys from a seed phrase using hashing (the BIP-32 standard). So a user can prove ownership by showing they know the seed, which an attacker who only cracked the elliptic-curve key would not have.

**The proposed steps:**
1. **Roll back** the blocks from after large-scale quantum theft became visible.
2. **Turn off ordinary transactions** from standard accounts (EOAs), since their signatures can no longer be trusted.
3. **Allow smart-contract-wallet transactions** instead, using account abstraction.
4. **Add a new transaction type** where users submit a zero-knowledge proof (a STARK, which is hash-based and quantum-safe) that they know the seed or hash preimage behind their key. Their account then switches to quantum-resistant verification code. Many proofs can be bundled together to keep fees down.

**Limitations:**
- It may be hard to tell exactly when the attack started, or whether a big transfer was theft or a legitimate trade.
- Rolling back blocks needs a lot of social agreement and would be disruptive.
- Keys that weren't made from a seed, such as some raw imported keys, may not be recoverable.
- Other cryptography in the protocol, like the BLS signatures validators use and KZG commitments, needs its own separate upgrade.

Over the longer term, Ethereum's roadmap aims to move to post-quantum signatures and account abstraction before this kind of emergency happens.
rubric: Emergency hard fork: roll back blocks after large-scale theft is detected, disable legacy ECDSA-signed transactions from EOAs
New transaction type where users prove knowledge of their seed/HD-wallet derivation (hash preimage) with a STARK, so hash-based secrets still protect funds
Longer term: move to quantum-resistant signatures (hash-based or lattice: ML-DSA/SLH-DSA/Falcon) and account abstraction
Notes funds in addresses that never exposed a public key are safer
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
This would require a major upgrade to the blockchain, as current ECDSA keypairs would be vulnerable. The chain could fork to adopt new keypairs, but this would be costly and complex. Users would need to migrate their funds to the new system, which would take time and resources. The transition would ensure long-term security against quantum attacks, but it would also require significant changes to the Ethereum network.

Specifically, people can merely sign messages committing to new quantum-resistant keypairs (or just higher-bit keypairs on similar algorithms), and the canonical chain can fork to make such keypairs valid. [3] What are the short term effects for a retail investor if the broker suddenly decided to allow close only for some positions?
The first point is a small inconvenience for me than a real issue since I mostly invest long term. However, it is not clear what are the consequences for the third point. units.question: What does EIP-4444 history expiry change for Ethereum node operators, and how much disk does it save?
units.gold:
EIP-4444 lets execution-layer nodes stop storing and serving old block history. In its current "partial" form, this means the block bodies and receipts from before the Merge (September 2022) can be deleted. That saves about **300–500 GB** of disk, enough that a full node fits comfortably on a **2 TB** drive.

**What changes for node operators**
- **What goes and what stays:** Pre-Merge bodies and receipts are removed. All headers are kept, so the chain can still be checked cryptographically back to genesis.
- **Why it's safe:** Proof-of-stake nodes sync from a recent checkpoint and don't need to re-execute every block from genesis.
- **All major clients support it (since July 8, 2025):**
  - Geth v1.16.0+: `geth prune-history` or `--history.chain postmerge`
  - Nethermind 1.32.2+: on by default for new syncs
  - Besu 25.7.0+: `besu storage prune-pre-merge-blocks` or `--history-expiry-prune`
  - Erigon v3.0.12+: `--history-expiry`
  - Reth v1.5.0+: `--prune.bodies.pre-merge`
- **Effect on RPC:** A pruned node can't return pre-Merge transactions, receipts or logs, for example old `eth_getLogs` ranges. Everyday activity like balances and transactions still works. If you need old data, you'll need an archive node or an external source.
- **Where old history lives now:** Institutional archive providers, torrents and the peer-to-peer network. Endpoints are listed at eth-clients.github.io/history-endpoints.

**Caveat:** The full version of EIP-4444 would delete history on a rolling basis, after a fixed retention window. When pruning was announced, that work was still "ongoing" with no timeline. I didn't check whether it has shipped since, so look at your client's release notes.
rubric: Nodes stop serving/storing historical blocks and receipts older than a cutoff; history moves to other distribution (e.g. Portal network, archives)
Partial history expiry (pre-Merge history) rolled out in July 2025; saves roughly 300-500 GB of disk
Consequence: syncing a full node fits well under 1 TB (he reports <0.5 TB with aggressive settings)
Old history is still available from other sources, not deleted from the world
units.answer: EIP-4444 introduces history expiry for Ethereum nodes, pruning blocks older than the consensus-layer retention window [2]. This reduces disk usage by removing historical data, saving users over 400GB of space [1]. The change allows nodes to discard code processing historical blocks, improving efficiency. The proposal aims to reduce network bandwidth by enabling lighter sync strategies based on PoS assumptions. [1]

Motivation: Historical blocks and receipts currently occupy more than 400GB of disk space (and growing!). By pruning the history, this proposal reduces the disk requirements for users. Pruning history also allows clients to remove code that processes historical blocks. Finally, this change will result in less bandwidth usage on the network as clients adopt more lightweight sync strategies based on the PoS weak subjectivity assumption.

[5] Data retention for EU citizens travelling between UK and EU during Brexit transition/implementation period
Answers > Answer (score 1): The current data retention policy has been created after much deliberation. I don’t see why it needs to be changed after Brexit. After all, even if not bound by EU laws, the Home Office will still have to abide by the UK’s own data protection laws. Any attempt to change retention policies will face strong criticism and legal challenge from privacy advocates.

The question that should be asked is “what will happen to data in post Brexit-UK that was collected before Brexit?” Again, this would only be an issue if there is a policy change.

A definitive answer can only be written after an explicit intention by the Home Office to change policy. Everything else is speculation.

[6] EMV
EMV is a standard protocol for credit cards and debit cards. These cards used to use a magnetic stripe to store information. This approach has two main problems: first, the amount of data that can be stored is relatively small. Such a card can store about 1024 Bits, or 128 bytes. The second problem is bigger: the data stored is not encrypted. Using a card with EMV technology, also called a "chip card" for the shiny, metallic "chip" on the front, can solve both problems: it can store much more data, and the data can be encrypted.

Payment cards that use chips have been in use since the early 1990s. Beforehand, each card issuer had their own protocol. With EMV, the protocol has been standardised. The first version of EMV was published in 1995, and there have been different versions since then. It was adopted in Europe before the United States, which required all new cards from 2015 on to have EMV chips.
